## Section 3.1: Logics

"Usually, a statement in a logic is written as

$$\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi$$

where $\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n$ and $\psi$ are propositions. Such a sequent expresses that $\psi$ follows (as conclusion) from the 
assumptions $\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n$. These propositions $\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n, \psi$ may contain (free) varaibles of certain types.
The context in which these variables are declared is left implicit $\dots$ . Contexts are very important in a categorical description of logic
$\dots$ therefore we prefer to use statements fo the form

$$\Gamma \ | \ \varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi$$

in which the context $\Gamma$ containing all the free variables of $\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_n$ and $\psi$ is written explicitly." - p.171

"Let $(\Sigma, \Box)$ be a specification for some system of logic, where $\Sigma$ is a many-typed signature and $\Box$ is something extra,
determined by the specific logic; it may consist of collections of additional atomic symbols and/or axioms $\dots$ . Given $\Sigma$ and $\Box$ 
we can start forming sequents. The categorical way to understand these sequents is as follows.

$$\overbrace{x_1: \sigma_1, \dots, x_n : \sigma_n}^{\text{index object in the base category}} \ | \ \underbrace{\varphi_1,\dots, \varphi_m \vdash \psi}_{\text{inequality} \ \leq \ \text{in the fibre over the index}} $$

" - p.173

## Section 4.1: Signatures, connectives and quantifiers

"In equational logic one only has equations

$$M =_{\sigma} M' $$

for terms $M$ and $M'$ of the same type $\sigma$, as (atomic) propositions." - p.221
